title: Quadratic Equations — Chapter Summary
intro: A quadratic equation in one variable is one that can be written as a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. This chapter develops three methods for solving such equations — factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula — uses the discriminant to predict the nature of the roots, and ends by translating short word problems into quadratic equations.

sections.heading: Standard form and roots
bullets: A quadratic equation in x is one that can be written a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a, b, c real and a ≠ 0.
Without a ≠ 0 the x^2 term disappears and the equation becomes linear.
A root is a value of x that makes the polynomial zero; geometrically, an x-intercept of y = a x^2 + b x + c.
A quadratic has at most two real roots.
Equations such as x + 6/x = 5 or √(x + 4) = x − 2 reduce to quadratics after clearing fractions or squaring; check every solution in the original equation.

sections.heading: Solution by factorisation
bullets: If a x^2 + b x + c = (p x + q)(r x + s) then either p x + q = 0 or r x + s = 0.
To factorise, find two numbers whose product is a × c and whose sum is b — the 'split-the-middle-term' trick.
Difference-of-squares pattern: x^2 − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3) → x = ±3.
Factorisation is the fastest method when integer factors of a × c summing to b are easy to spot.

sections.heading: Completing the square
bullets: Key identity: x^2 + 2 p x = (x + p)^2 − p^2.
Algorithm: divide by a, move the constant, add (b/(2a))^2 to both sides, take square roots, solve for x.
The method works even when factorisation does not.
Carrying it out on the general form a x^2 + b x + c = 0 produces the quadratic formula.

sections.heading: Quadratic formula (Sridharacharya)
bullets: x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4 a c)) / (2 a) for any quadratic equation in standard form.
Known to Sridharacharya in the 9th century; sometimes called the Sridharacharya formula.
Sum and product of roots: α + β = −b/a, α β = c/a.
Given roots p, q the equation is x^2 − (p + q) x + p q = 0.

sections.heading: Nature of roots — the discriminant
bullets: D = b^2 − 4 a c is the discriminant.
D > 0: two distinct real roots (parabola crosses x-axis at two points).
D = 0: one repeated real root x = −b / (2 a) (parabola touches x-axis).
D < 0: no real roots (parabola lies entirely above or below the axis).
If a, b, c are rational, the real roots are rational iff D is a perfect square.

sections.heading: Word problems
bullets: Standard four-step recipe: (i) name the unknown, (ii) translate the conditions to a quadratic, (iii) solve, (iv) reject roots that contradict the situation.
Geometry: rectangle with area 60 and length 4 more than breadth → x^2 + 4 x − 60 = 0 → breadth 6 m.
Speed–time: 360 km journey taking 1 h less when speed rises by 5 → x^2 + 5 x − 1800 = 0 → 40 km/h.
Number relations: number plus reciprocal = 13/6 → 6 x^2 − 13 x + 6 = 0 → x = 2/3 or 3/2.
Always discard negative lengths, ages or speeds — even when they are formal solutions.

key_takeaways: Standard form a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 is the gateway to every method.
Three equivalent solving methods: factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula.
x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4 a c)) / (2 a) — the quadratic (Sridharacharya) formula — works for every quadratic.
The discriminant D = b^2 − 4 a c determines the nature of the roots: D > 0 / = 0 / < 0.
Sum α + β = −b/a, product α β = c/a; from given roots p, q the equation is x^2 − (p + q) x + p q = 0.
Word problems: model carefully, solve, and always discard roots that the physical situation rules out.

glossary.definition: An equation that can be written a x^2 + b x + c = 0 with a, b, c real and a ≠ 0.
The coefficient a of x^2 in the standard form a x^2 + b x + c = 0.
A value of x that makes a x^2 + b x + c equal to zero.
If a product of real numbers is zero then at least one of the factors is zero — the basis for solving by factorisation.
Writing b as the sum of two numbers whose product is a × c so that a x^2 + b x + c factors as a product of two linear terms.
Rewriting a x^2 + b x + c = 0 as (x + b/(2a))^2 = (b^2 − 4 a c)/(4 a^2) and solving by taking square roots.
x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4 a c)) / (2 a); gives both roots of any quadratic in standard form.
D = b^2 − 4 a c; its sign determines whether the roots are real-distinct, real-equal, or non-real.
A root that arises from a perfect-square factor; happens iff D = 0, with x = −b / (2 a).
If α, β are roots of a x^2 + b x + c = 0 then α + β = −b/a.
If α, β are roots of a x^2 + b x + c = 0 then α × β = c/a.
A value that satisfies an equation obtained by squaring or multiplying by an unknown but not the original equation; must be discarded after checking.
